name: Hooker's Green
lede: Hooker's Green is a deep, cool watercolour green mixed from gamboge and Prussian blue or indigo, named for the English botanical artist who used it to paint leaves.

sections.title: A painter's mixed green
sections.body:
The pigment compendium groups Hooker's Green with the nineteenth-century "mixed greens": not one substance but a blend, in this case the yellow resin [[gamboge-yellow|gamboge]] cut with [[prussian-blue]] or [[indigo]] [1]. The nearest named color on file is [[light-danube-green]], 2.6 ΔE off [1][2].

It takes its name from William Hooker, a botanical artist for the Royal Horticultural Society, who mixed gamboge with a little Prussian blue to get a green suited to painting foliage [3]. The mix worked best as a watercolour; some Flemish oil painters used it too, and Rembrandt is said to have liked gamboge for the golden cast it took on in oil [4][5]. Gamboge's resin grains later had an odd second life: the physicist Jean Perrin used them in 1908 to demonstrate Brownian motion, part of the evidence for the existence of atoms [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: ColorHub's reference swatch sits at lightness 47, chroma 20, hue 173 degrees, a muted blue-green [6]. Its nearest library name is Light Danube Green, about 2.6 units away, with Jasper Green close behind [6]. Ridgway's 1912 standards list it on plate XIX, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 carries it as block 164 [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this green, as photographed, in 76 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.3 percent [7]. It covers nearly half the canvas in two Klimt garden paintings, *Avenue in the Park of Schloss Kammer* (1912) and *Park at Kammer Castle* (1909), and almost 40 percent of Caillebotte's *Skiffs* (1877) [7]. The earliest dated match is Hans Memling's 1480 portrait of an unknown man with a letter, where it covers 16 percent of the canvas, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [7]. These are computed color matches on aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [7].
